title: "Lighting and shading"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5,
  dpi = 150,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE
)
```

```{r setup}
library(ggcube)
library(patchwork)
theme_set(theme_gray())
theme_update(axis.text = element_blank(),
             axis.title = element_blank())
```

Lighting modifies the fill and/or color of polygon faces based on their orientation
relative to a light source, giving surfaces and volumes a sense of depth and shape.
ggcube's lighting system only renders **form** shadows, not **cast** shadows. Lighting 
can be applied to any polygon-based 3D layer --- surfaces, hulls, bars, voxels, and 
polygon text --- but is useful mainly for layers where polygon orientation varies. 

Lighting colors each face in three steps. First, the angle between the face and the
direction toward the light is measured. Then a *ramp* turns that angle into how far
the face moves toward shadow or highlight: by default, faces at 45 degrees to the light
keep exactly the color you gave them, faces turned further toward the light are
highlighted, and faces turned further away are shadowed. Finally, a *tone* decides what
lighter and darker look like for a given color: by default, colors become lighter and
darker versions of the same hue.

This vignette covers how to control [what parts](#lighting-targets) of your plot lighting 
is applied to, how to change the [visual qualities](#light-qualities) of the lighting, how
to change the direction of the [light source](#light-sources), how to control how the
[underside](#backface-lighting) of a polygon is lit, and how lighting is shown in
[guides](#3d-guides).

We'll use a common base plot throughout: a sphere, drawn as an isosurface of a function of
x, y, and z. Here it is with default lighting:

```{r base}
# a unit sphere, centered at x = x0
sphere <- function(x0 = 0, n = 40, ...) {
  geom_isofunction_3d(fun = function(x, y, z) (x - x0)^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 1,
                      xlim = x0 + c(-1.1, 1.1), ylim = c(-1.1, 1.1), zlim = c(-1.1, 1.1),
                      n = n, ...)
}

p <- ggplot() +
  sphere(fill = "#9e2602") +
  coord_3d(scales = "fixed")
p
```



## Lighting targets

Lighting can be set at two levels:

- **Plot-level**: adding `light(...)` to a plot applies it to all layers. It can appear
  anywhere in the plot expression, before or after `coord_3d()`. (Lighting can also be
  passed to `coord_3d(light = ...)`, which is useful when you want a reusable coord
  object that carries its own lighting; supplying it in both places is an error.)
- **Layer-level**: `geom_*_3d(light = light(...))` overrides the plot-level setting for
  that layer.

Use `light("none")` to disable lighting entirely, or `light = NULL` in a layer to
inherit the plot-level setting (the default layer behavior). Here we add a second
layer to our plot, and override the inherited light settings to disable lighting for 
this layer:

```{r where}
p + sphere(x0 = 2.5, fill = "#9e2602", light = "none")
```

The `fill` and `color` parameters control which aesthetics get modified by lighting. 
By default both are `TRUE`. Here a coarser sphere is outlined in white, which is lit along
with the fill by default, and stays white with `color = FALSE`:

```{r targets, fig.height = 3.5}
pw <- ggplot() +
  sphere(n = 12, fill = "#9e2602", color = "white", linewidth = .3) +
  coord_3d(scales = "fixed")
(pw + ggtitle("fill + color (default)")) +
  (pw + light(fill = TRUE, color = FALSE) + ggtitle("fill only"))
```

When no color is given, polygon layers outline polygons in their fill color, which hides the
seams between them. These outlines are always lit along with the fill.

Lighting works with both solid and aesthetically-mapped colors:

```{r mapped_colors}
ggplot() +
  sphere(mapping = aes(fill = after_stat(x))) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  coord_3d(scales = "fixed")
```

Contours (`geom_contour_3d()`) and ridgelines (`geom_ridgeline_3d()`) are the exception
to default lighting: their faces all point the same way, so lighting could only shift all
their colors away from those you gave them. They are lit only when you set lighting
explicitly, with `+ light()` or their `light` argument.

## Light qualities

### Shadow and highlight strength

`shadow` and `highlight` set how strong shadows and highlights are, from 0 (none) to 1
(fully black or white, with the default tone). By default, shadows are stronger than
highlights (`shadow = 0.8`, `highlight = 0.6`), since fading to black looks more natural
than fading to white:

```{r strength, fig.height = 3}
(p + light(shadow = 0.4, highlight = 0.3) + ggtitle("subtle")) +
  (p + ggtitle("default")) +
  (p + light(shadow = 1, highlight = 0.9) + ggtitle("strong")) +
  plot_layout(ncol = 3)
```

### Ramps

Lighting ramps control how brightness changes as a surface turns away from the light:

- **`"smooth"`** (default): Brightness changes gradually. Only surfaces pointing directly
  away from the light source are fully shadowed.
- **`"hard"`**: All surfaces angled 90 degrees or more from the light are fully shadowed,
  giving a sharp edge between lit and unlit sides.
- **`"steps"`**: Brightness is discretized into flat bands, for a cartoon-like look.
- **`"none"`**: Disables lighting across the plot, except for layers that declare it
  themselves.

```{r ramps, fig.height = 3}
(p + ggtitle('"smooth" (default)')) +
  (p + light("hard") + ggtitle('"hard"')) +
  (p + light("steps") + ggtitle('"steps"')) +
  plot_layout(ncol = 3)
```

For more control, you can give a ramp object instead of a name: `ramp_smooth()`, `ramp_hard()`, and
`ramp_steps()` take a `neutral` angle, at which faces keep their base color, and
`ramp_steps()` takes the number of bands, `n`. A smaller `neutral` angle puts the base
color on faces closer to facing the light, which darkens the plot overall:

```{r ramp-options, fig.height = 3}
(p + light(ramp_smooth(neutral = 30)) + ggtitle("ramp_smooth(neutral = 30)")) +
  (p + light(ramp_smooth(neutral = 60)) + ggtitle("ramp_smooth(neutral = 60)")) +
  (p + light(ramp_steps(n = 3)) + ggtitle("ramp_steps(n = 3)")) +
  plot_layout(ncol = 3)
```

### Tones

A lighting "tone" decides what lighter and darker look like for a given base color:

- **`"lightness"`** (default): Colors become lighter and darker versions of the same hue,
  reaching white at full highlight and black at full shadow. Lightness is changed in the
  perceptual OKLab color space, which preserves hue as colors lighten and darken.
- **`"tint"`**: Colors mix toward a chosen highlight color and shadow color, for colored
  light.
- **`"normals"`**: Faces are colored by the direction they face, replacing the base colors
  entirely.

Give `tone_tint()` its colors to choose the color of the light. Warm highlights with cool
shadows are a classic choice:

```{r tones, fig.height = 3}
(p + ggtitle('"lightness" (default)')) +
  (p + light(tone = tone_tint(shadow = "darkblue", highlight = "gold")) +
      ggtitle("tone_tint()")) +
  (p + light(tone = "normals") + ggtitle('"normals"')) +
  plot_layout(ncol = 3)
```



## Light sources

### Direction and anchoring

The `direction` parameter is a length-3 vector specifying where light comes from; for example, 
`direction = c(0, -1, 0)` lights the plot from the negative y direction. The `anchor` parameter 
controls whether this direction is relative to the data axes or the camera:

- **`anchor = "scene"`** (default): Direction is relative to the data axes and rotates
  with the plot. `direction = c(1, 0, 0)` always lights surfaces facing the "xmax" face.
- **`anchor = "camera"`**: Direction is fixed relative to the viewing pane.
  `direction = c(1, 0, 0)` always lights surfaces facing the right side of the plot,
  regardless of rotation.

```{r direction, fig.height = 3.5}
(p + light("hard", direction = c(0, -1, 0)) + ggtitle('anchor = "scene"')) +
  (p + light("hard", direction = c(0, -1, 0), anchor = "camera") +
      ggtitle('anchor = "camera"'))
```

Directions can also be given as angles with `direction()`, which takes an
azimuth (a compass bearing, measured clockwise from the positive y axis) and an
elevation (degrees above the xy plane). This is often easier when you want to
raise or lower a light without changing which side it comes from. The default light
comes from the negative x side (an azimuth of 270), 60 degrees above the horizon. Here it
is low and then overhead:

```{r direction-angles, fig.height = 3.5}
(p + light("hard", direction = direction(270, 10)) + ggtitle("elevation 10")) +
  (p + light("hard", direction = direction(270, 90)) + ggtitle("elevation 90"))
```

Printing a light shows its direction both ways, which can help in translating
between the two:

```{r print-light}
light(direction = c(-1, -1, 1))
```

To compare light directions side by side, or to move the light around
interactively, see the `light_azimuth` and `light_elevation` arguments of
`orbit_3d()` and `animate_3d()`, and the view facets `facet_wrap_views()` and
`facet_grid_views()`, covered in the
[animation and multiple views](../articles/animation.html) article.


### Positional lighting

In addition to directional lighting (parallel rays from a direction), ggcube also supports
positional lighting from a point source. Use `position` instead of `direction` to specify
a light source location in data coordinates. Setting `distance_falloff = TRUE` applies 
inverse-square intensity falloff from the light source position.

```{r positional}
ggplot(mountain, aes(x, y, z)) +
  stat_surface_3d(fill = "red", color = "red") +
  coord_3d(
    light = light(position = c(.5, .7, 95), distance_falloff = TRUE),
    ratio = c(1.5, 2, 1))
```


## Backface lighting

A backface is the side of a polygon facing the underside of a surface or the inside of a
volume. By default, backfaces receive inverted lighting relative to frontfaces 
(`backface_scale = -1`), creating strong visual contrast between the two sides. 
Setting `backface_scale = 1` lights backfaces the same as frontfaces. Modifying 
`backface_offset` to uniformly darkens or brightens all backfaces.


```{r backface, fig.height = 3}
pb <- ggplot() +
  geom_function_3d(fun = function(x, y) x^2 + y^2,
                   xlim = c(-3, 3), ylim = c(-3, 3),
                   fill = "steelblue", color = "steelblue") +
      coord_3d(pitch = 0, roll = -70, yaw = 0)

(pb +
    ggtitle("default:\nbackface_scale = -1\nbackface_offset = 0")) +
  (pb + light(backface_scale = 1) +
      ggtitle("\nbackface_scale = 1\nbackface_offset = 0")) +
  (pb + light(backface_scale = 1, backface_offset = -.5) +
      ggtitle("\nbackface_scale = 1\nbackface_offset = -0.5")) +
  plot_layout(nrow = 1)
```



## 3D guides

When lighting is active, standard color guides don't reflect the range of shaded colors
visible in the plot. So when lighting applies to a layer that maps `fill` or `color`, ggcube
uses `guide_colorbar_3d()` and `guide_legend_3d()` in place of the standard guides, showing
the shading gradient alongside each color, with the colors as given in the middle:

```{r guide_colorbar}
ggplot(mountain, aes(x, y, z, fill = z)) +
  stat_surface_3d() +
  light(direction = c(1, 0, 0)) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = c("tomato", "dodgerblue")) +
  coord_3d(ratio = c(2, 3, 1.5))
```

```{r guide_legend}
ggplot(mountain, aes(x, y, z, fill = x > .5, group = 1)) +
  stat_surface_3d() +
  light(direction = c(1, 0, 0)) +
  coord_3d(ratio = c(2, 3, 1.5))
```

Call the guides yourself to change their options: both accept `shade_range` to control the
range of shading shown (a length-2 vector from -1, full shadow, to 1, full highlight), and
`reverse_shade` to flip the gradient direction. For an unshaded guide, ask for a standard
one, e.g. `guides(fill = "colourbar")`.

```{r guide_options}
ggplot(mountain, aes(x, y, z, fill = z)) +
  stat_surface_3d() +
  light(direction = c(1, 0, 0)) +
  guides(fill = guide_colorbar_3d(shade_range = c(-1, 1))) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = c("tomato", "dodgerblue")) +
  coord_3d(ratio = c(2, 3, 1.5))
```

Note that when fill and color map to the same variable, ggplot2 creates a shared scale.
In this case, set the 3D guide's options via `guides(fill = guide_colorbar_3d())`, not via
the color guide.
